tracks.title: Shared Fundamentals
tracks.description: Listening, rhythm, EQ, and structure — required before DJ or Production deep work.

tracks.title: DJ Track
tracks.description: From installing free DJ software to recording your first 10–15 minute mix.

tracks.title: Production Track
tracks.description: From picking a free DAW to exporting your first finished track.

modules.title: Start Here
modules.description: Orientation, safe listening habits, and a simple 30-day practice contract.

lessons.title: Welcome to BeatPath
lessons.summary: BeatPath is your one hub from absolute beginner to a first DJ mix and a first finished track. You will learn in small steps with practice built in.
whyItMatters: One clear path beats fifty random YouTube tabs.
Progress is saved on this device — no account needed for v1.

exercise.title: Set your intention
exercise.description: Open Today's Practice, pick a daily time window (e.g. 8:00–8:30 PM IST), and choose to begin with Shared Fundamentals.

checklist: I understand BeatPath covers both DJ and production
I set (or wrote down) a daily practice time
I will start with Shared modules before buying gear
lessons.successCheckpoint: Daily time chosen; Shared path selected

lessons.title: How to listen like a maker
lessons.summary: Passive listening is enjoyment. Active listening is study: you notice when the kick enters, when the bass drops out, and when energy rises or falls.
whyItMatters: DJs use this to plan transitions.
Producers use this to copy structure without copying melodies.

exercise.title: Mark three songs
exercise.description: Pick 3 tracks you like. For each, note: approx BPM feel (slow/medium/fast), where the first big energy change is, and whether drums stay constant.

checklist: I wrote one sentence: what I want my first mix or track to feel like

lessons.title: Headphones, volume, and hearing safety
lessons.summary: Loud volume feels exciting and destroys detail (and hearing). Keep sessions reasonable and take breaks.
whyItMatters: You cannot DJ or produce well with damaged ears.

exercise.title: Safe session setup
exercise.description: Set device volume to a comfortable speech-level for podcasts, then music slightly above that — not max. Plan a max 60-minute focused block with a 5-minute quiet break.

checklist: I know the 60-minute focus + break rule
I will use headphones that seal enough to hear bass without blasting

lessons.title: Free tools you will use (overview)
lessons.summary: Day 1 needs software, not a ₹40,000 controller. Mixxx is free and open source for DJing. For production, pick one free DAW later in Module M6.
whyItMatters: Buying gear too early delays practice.

exercise.title: Bookmark your toolkit
exercise.description: Bookmark Mixxx download page and skim the DAW comparison page inside BeatPath (/software). Do not install everything today — just know where things live.

checklist: I will install DJ software in Module M4 and one DAW in Module M6

lessons.title: Your 30-day practice contract
lessons.summary: Consistency beats intensity. Thirty days of 20–40 minutes will outrun one heroic weekend.
whyItMatters: Goals should be observable (record a mix), not vague (get good).

exercise.title: Write three goals
exercise.description: Write: (1) habit goal — practice N days/week, (2) DJ goal — e.g. beatmatch two tracks, (3) production goal — e.g. 8-bar drum loop. Keep them small.

modules.title: Rhythm & Pulse
modules.description: BPM, bars, drum alphabet, and groove — the shared language of DJs and producers.

lessons.title: What is BPM?
lessons.summary: BPM means beats per minute — how fast the pulse is. House often sits near 120–130; hip-hop often slower; drum & bass much faster.
whyItMatters: Matching BPM is the first half of beatmatching.
Producers set project BPM so drums grid correctly.

exercise.title: Tap tempo on five songs
exercise.description: Use the BeatPath metronome tap feature (or tap along) on 5 songs. Guess slow/medium/fast, then check any BPM shown in files/apps if available.

checklist: I can explain BPM in one sentence
I know my favorite genre's usual BPM range roughly

lessons.title: Beats, bars, and counting to 8
lessons.summary: In most dance music, you count 1-2-3-4 in a bar, and group bars into phrases of 8 or 16. DJs change tracks on phrase boundaries so the floor feels natural.
whyItMatters: Phrasing separates beginner mashups from smooth sets.
Producers arrange drops on phrase starts.

exercise.title: Count eight-bar phrases
exercise.description: Start metronome at 120 BPM. Count bars: each 4 beats = 1 bar. Clap lightly on bar 1 of every 8 bars. Do this for 2 minutes without losing count.

checklist: I counted at least four clean 8-bar cycles
I tried counting along to one real song

lessons.title: Kick, snare, hat — the drum alphabet
lessons.summary: Kick (bass drum) is the thump on the pulse. Snare/clap often hits on beats 2 and 4. Hats tick the subdivisions. If you can name them by ear, everything else gets easier.
whyItMatters: Critical for beatmatching and for programming drums.
Ear training compounds quickly with short daily drills.

exercise.title: Drum ID trainer
exercise.description: Complete 20 rounds in /practice/ear-drums. Aim for 80%+ correctness. Repeat tomorrow if needed.

checklist: Scored at least 80% or scheduled a retry
I can hum a kick vs snare difference

lessons.title: Groove vs metronome
lessons.summary: A metronome is perfect pulse. Groove is how drums sit around that pulse — especially the snare/clap on 2 and 4 (backbeat) and hat swing.
whyItMatters: Lifeless grids can be tightened later; feel comes first.

exercise.title: Clap the backbeat
exercise.description: Metronome on. Clap only on beats 2 and 4 for 60 seconds. Then add quiet foot taps on 1 and 3.

checklist: Felt the difference between all-four stomps and backbeat

lessons.title: Genre tempo map
lessons.summary: Rough map: Hip-hop ~80–100, Bollywood/pop dance often ~100–130, House/techno ~120–135, Drum & bass ~160–175. Maps are guides, not laws.
whyItMatters: Crate building and playlist energy depend on tempo neighborhoods.
Helps you avoid impossible mixes on Day 1.

exercise.title: Sort eight tracks
exercise.description: Take 8 songs from your phone. Sort into Slow / Mid / Fast piles. Note one track you would never mix into another (tempo clash).

checklist: I know which pile I want for my first DJ crate

lessons.title: Drill week: daily 10-min pulse
lessons.summary: Short daily reps beat long rare sessions. This lesson is a repeating drill template.

exercise.title: 10-minute pulse drill
exercise.description: 5 min metronome counting bars; 5 min ear-drums or beat-pad. Log five days (need not be consecutive).

modules.title: Sound, Frequency & EQ
modules.description: Hear bass/mids/highs, understand clashing low end, and use EQ as a clarity tool.

lessons.title: Bass, mids, and highs in plain English
lessons.summary: Bass is the weight (kick, sub bass). Mids carry vocals and most instruments. Highs are sparkle (hats, air). EQ turns these bands up or down.
whyItMatters: DJs carve bass so two tracks do not fight.
Producers carve space so every part is audible.

exercise.title: EQ demo — solo bands
exercise.description: Open /practice/eq-demo. Solo low, then mid, then high. Say out loud what instruments live in each band.

checklist: I can point to where the kick lives
I can point to where hats live

lessons.title: Why two basslines clash
lessons.summary: Low frequencies need space. Two full basslines together turn to mud. Classic DJ move: reduce bass on the incoming track until the swap, then restore.
whyItMatters: Same idea in production: kick and bass share a plan.

exercise.title: Bass kill practice
exercise.description: In /practice/crossfader (or EQ demo with two loops if crossfader not ready: simulate by cutting low on one source), practice bringing track B in with bass down, then swap bass to B.

resources.title: Mixxx wiki — How To Match Beats (structure notes)

lessons.title: EQ for clarity, not more
lessons.summary: Beginners boost everything. Pros often cut a little mud (roughly 200–400 Hz) and gently shape. Small moves.
whyItMatters: Boosting all bands is just volume.

exercise.title: Prefer a cut
exercise.description: On the EQ demo, boost mids hard (notice harshness), reset, then try a gentle low-mid cut. Prefer the clearer version.

checklist: I will default to small EQ moves

lessons.title: Loudness vs quality
lessons.summary: Phone speakers hide bass and exaggerate mids. Club systems reveal low-end chaos. Always check on more than one device later.
whyItMatters: Protects you from over-boosting bass on headphones.

exercise.title: Two-device listen
exercise.description: Play the same commercial track on laptop/headphones and on phone speaker. Note three differences.

checklist: I know phone bass is unreliable

lessons.title: Ear drill: where is the hat?
lessons.summary: Train yourself to locate hats and air in the high band quickly — useful when EQing live or mixing.

exercise.title: Band hunt
exercise.description: EQ demo: randomly cut one band, guess which. Ten rounds. Optionally visit EarQuiz later.

modules.title: Structure, Phrasing & Energy
modules.description: Hear phrases and energy curves — the bridge between DJing and arranging.

lessons.title: Phrases: 8 / 16 / 32 bars
lessons.summary: Dance music is built from phrases. Mix in on phrase starts; arrange drops on phrase starts.

exercise.title: Phrase map two tracks
exercise.description: In two dance tracks, mark (timestamp or tally) where you feel a new phrase. Confirm they often land every 8 or 16 bars.

checklist: I can explain phrase in one sentence

lessons.title: Intro, break, drop, outro
lessons.summary: Many electronic tracks: intro (mix-friendly), groove, break/build, drop, outro. Names vary; energy shape matters more than labels.
whyItMatters: DJs use intros/outros as mixing runways.
Producers copy shapes before inventing new ones.

exercise.title: Label one reference
exercise.description: Pick one track. Label sections: intro / main / break / drop / outro (skip what does not apply).

checklist: I noted the longest mix-friendly stretch

lessons.title: Energy curves for DJs and producers
lessons.summary: A set or song is an energy journey. Flat energy bores; random spikes confuse. Sketch curves on purpose.

exercise.title: Draw one curve
exercise.description: On paper or notes, draw energy (low→high) across your reference track's sections.

lessons.title: Arrangement is storytelling
lessons.summary: A loop is a sentence. Arrangement is the story: bring elements in/out over 32 bars.

exercise.title: 32-bar story on beat pad
exercise.description: Make an 8-bar drum loop, then vary it across 32 bars (hats in/out, snare variation). Use /practice/beat-pad or Learning Music.

checklist: I noticed when it got boring and changed something

lessons.title: Shared fundamentals exam
lessons.summary: Quick check before DJ and Production tracks unlock fully. This is a confidence gate, not a punishment.

exercise.title: Mixed quiz + listening
exercise.description: Self-check: (1) define BPM, bar, phrase; (2) ID kick/snare/hat in ear trainer ≥80%; (3) explain bass clash; (4) mark a phrase in one song. Retake any weak lesson.

checklist: I feel ready for DJ and/or Production modules

modules.title: DJ Software & Library
modules.description: Install free DJ software, learn deck layout, and build a tiny starter crate.

lessons.title: DJ software overview
lessons.summary: Mixxx is free/open source and enough to learn everything. Serato DJ Lite, rekordbox, and VirtualDJ Home are free tiers of commercial apps. Concepts transfer.
whyItMatters: Pick one and stick with it for 30 days.

exercise.title: Choose and install
exercise.description: Install Mixxx (recommended) or one free commercial lite version. Open it once successfully.

lessons.title: First look: decks, cue, play
lessons.summary: Two decks (or more). Load a track, set a cue point at the start of the usable intro, practice play/pause.
whyItMatters: Cue points are your bookmarks under pressure.
Layout familiarity is half of DJing.

exercise.title: Load two tracks
exercise.description: Load Track A and B. Set a cue near the start of each. Play A on master; browse B.

lessons.title: Building a starter crate
lessons.summary: Ten to twenty tracks in one energy neighborhood beat a chaotic 2000-song library.

exercise.title: Crate of 10+
exercise.description: Create a playlist/crate with ≥10 tracks you would actually play. Prefer mid-tempo dance/EDM/house/Bollywood-EDM you know. Note BPM if the software shows it.

checklist: I removed anything with huge tempo outliers

lessons.title: Headphones vs master / cue mix
lessons.summary: Master is what the room hears. Headphones preview the next track. Cue mix blends them for your ears.
whyItMatters: Audience should not hear your scrubbing.

exercise.title: Practice cue mix
exercise.description: Play A on master. Cue B in headphones only. Flip cue mix and confirm B is not on master.

checklist: I can find cue gain/mix quickly

lessons.title: Hot cues and loops
lessons.summary: Hot cues jump to moments (drop, vocal). Loops hold a section to extend intros/outros while you prepare.
whyItMatters: Creative tool later; utility tool now.

exercise.title: Two cues + one loop
exercise.description: On one track: cue at intro, cue at drop. Make an 8-bar loop on a clean drum section and exit the loop cleanly.

lessons.title: Sync button: friend and trap
lessons.summary: Sync matches tempo (and sometimes beats) automatically. Use it to learn phrasing and EQ — but also practice without it so you are not helpless when Sync fails.

exercise.title: One with, one without
exercise.description: Do a short transition using Sync. Then attempt tempo match manually (even if messy). Write one sentence on what Sync hid from you.

modules.title: Beatmatching & Transitions
modules.description: Tempo match, nudge, ride pitch, phrase blends, and EQ bass swaps.

lessons.title: Beatmatching: tempo first
lessons.summary: Before beats align, tempos must match. Use the pitch/tempo fader until BPMs agree (by ear or display, then trust ear).

exercise.title: Match B to A
exercise.description: Play A. Adjust B's tempo until it feels the same speed for 30 seconds.

checklist: Tempos matched by ear or display+ear
I know where the pitch fader is without looking

lessons.title: Nudging into alignment
lessons.summary: Once tempos match, nudge (jog / bend) so downbeats land together. Classic drill: same track on both decks.

exercise.title: Same-track lock
exercise.description: Load the same track on A and B. Match tempo, align beats, keep locked for 16 bars.

lessons.title: Riding the pitch
lessons.summary: Tracks drift. Tiny pitch rides keep alignment. Look less; listen more.

exercise.title: Stay locked 32 bars
exercise.description: Different tracks, similar BPM. Keep kick alignment for 32 bars using small corrections.

checklist: Corrections were small, not panic scratches

lessons.title: Phrased transitions
lessons.summary: Start the incoming track so its phrase lines up with the outgoing phrase. Dowbeats and musical sentences agree.
whyItMatters: This is what makes mixes feel intentional.

exercise.title: Three phrased blends
exercise.description: Perform 3 transitions that begin on phrase boundaries. Record mentally which ones felt smooth.

lessons.title: EQ bass swap transition
lessons.summary: During the blend, keep only one full bassline. Swap bass as you hand over the groove.
whyItMatters: Protects the PA and the dancefloor.

exercise.title: Clean bass swap
exercise.description: In a phrased blend, cut bass on B until swap point, then cut bass on A as you restore B. Repeat 3 times.

lessons.title: Filters and FX tastefully
lessons.summary: Filters and effects are seasoning. One intentional sweep beats five gimmicks.

exercise.title: One sweep rule
exercise.description: Do a full transition using at most one filter sweep and no other FX. Listen back if you can record.

lessons.title: Drill: 15-min transition gym
lessons.summary: Repeated short sessions beat occasional long ones.
whyItMatters: Prepares you for the capstone mix.

exercise.title: Transition gym ×5
exercise.description: Fifteen minutes: only two-track transitions (tempo, phrase, bass swap). Complete five sessions.

modules.title: Production: DAW Basics
modules.description: Pick one DAW, learn timeline/MIDI/mixer, and export a test file.

lessons.title: DAW comparison (free and popular)
lessons.summary: Free starters: LMMS (cross-platform), Cakewalk (Windows), Waveform Free, Audacity (editing), Reaper (eval, cheap license). Popular paid: FL Studio, Ableton Live, Logic (Mac). Pick ONE for 30 days.
whyItMatters: Concepts transfer after one workflow clicks.

exercise.title: Pick one
exercise.description: Read /software and choose one DAW. Write why in one line (OS + budget + genre interest).

lessons.title: Install and first project
lessons.summary: Install, create empty project, set BPM to something you like (e.g. 120), save a template.

exercise.title: Template save
exercise.description: Create project, set BPM, add 2–4 empty tracks labeled Drums/Bass/Music/FX, save as Template-BeatPath.

lessons.title: Timeline, tracks, clips/patterns
lessons.summary: Music is laid on a timeline. Clips/patterns are blocks you repeat and arrange.

exercise.title: Four bar markers
exercise.description: Place markers or empty clips at bars 1, 9, 17, 25. Scroll and zoom comfortably.

checklist: I know how to loop a region for editing

lessons.title: MIDI vs audio
lessons.summary: MIDI is notes/data that drive instruments. Audio is recorded sound. Drums and synths often start as MIDI; vocals/samples as audio.
whyItMatters: Editing notes is easier than re-recording sometimes.

exercise.title: Draw middle C
exercise.description: Add a software instrument, draw a MIDI note (middle C), make it play on loop.

lessons.title: Mixer: faders, pan, mute/solo
lessons.summary: Mixing starts with volume balance and pan. Mute/solo helps you focus.
whyItMatters: Good levels solve half of 'my track sounds bad'.

exercise.title: Balance three parts
exercise.description: Put kick, hat, and a tone on three tracks. Balance so kick is clearest, hat supports, tone not screaming.

lessons.title: Export settings (WAV/MP3)
lessons.summary: Export/render bounces your project to a file. WAV is higher quality for archiving; MP3 is smaller for sharing.
whyItMatters: You cannot improve what you never export.

exercise.title: 10-second export
exercise.description: Export at least 10 seconds to WAV or MP3 and play it outside the DAW (phone/files app).

checklist: I know where exports are saved

modules.title: Beat Making, Bass & Melody
modules.description: Program drums, add bass and a simple hook, arrange to 32 bars with legal samples.

lessons.title: Program a 4-on-the-floor kick
lessons.summary: Four-on-the-floor: kick on every beat. House/EDM foundation. Also practice in BeatPath beat pad.

exercise.title: Kick every beat
exercise.description: In DAW or /practice/beat-pad, place kicks on all four beats; loop 8 bars cleanly.

lessons.title: Snare/clap + hats
lessons.summary: Add snare/clap on 2 and 4; hats on 8th notes (or offbeats).
whyItMatters: Completes the drum alphabet in practice.

exercise.title: Full basic kit
exercise.description: Add backbeat + hats to your kick loop. Listen for clutter; simplify if needed.

lessons.title: Ghost notes and swing (light)
lessons.summary: Swing delays some hats/notes for human feel. Ghost notes are quiet extra hits. Use lightly.

exercise.title: Add light swing
exercise.description: Enable swing ~55–60% or nudge hats slightly. A/B with straight timing.

checklist: Kept the one that feels better

lessons.title: Bass that follows the kick
lessons.summary: Write a simple bass on root notes. Side-plan with kick: leave space or duck later. For now, avoid long bass notes on every kick collision if muddy.
whyItMatters: Low-end clarity is pro territory even for beginners.

exercise.title: Root-note bass
exercise.description: Add a bass instrument; play roots that fit your drums in one key. Check with EQ ears: if muddy, shorten bass notes.

lessons.title: One-scale melody (minor pentatonic)
lessons.summary: Minor pentatonic is beginner-friendly. Limit yourself to 5 notes; write an 8-bar hook you can hum.
whyItMatters: Hooks > complex runs for first tracks.

exercise.title: Humable hook
exercise.description: Write 8 bars using a pentatonic scale (DAW scale mode or Learning Music). Hum it without looking.

lessons.title: Sampling ethics and free packs
lessons.summary: Only use samples you have rights to: bundled DAW content, clearly free/CC0 packs, or your recordings. Do not rip copyrighted songs for 'my beat' uploads.

exercise.title: Get one legal pack
exercise.description: Download one free sample pack from a reputable free source or use stock sounds in your DAW. Install/tag it.

checklist: Legal pack or stock library ready
I understand not to pirate packs/courses
I labeled a favorite kick and snare

lessons.title: From loop to 32 bars
lessons.summary: Duplicate your loop and change something every 8 bars: hats filter, bass rest, melody entry.

exercise.title: 32-bar sketch
exercise.description: Arrange intro drums → full groove → melody entry across 32 bars. Export a rough bounce.

resources.title: freeCodeCamp FL Studio course (optional parallel video)

modules.title: DJ Capstone: First Mix
modules.description: Plan, practice, record, critique, and re-record a 10–15 minute continuous mix.

lessons.title: Planning a 10–15 min set
lessons.summary: Write track order and intended transition type (phrase + bass swap). Keep 4–6 tracks.

exercise.title: Set card
exercise.description: On paper: track list, BPM notes, where you will mix (intro→outro).

lessons.title: Practice run (no record)
lessons.summary: Full run without recording pressure. Note weak spots only.

exercise.title: Full unrecorded run
exercise.description: Play the planned set start to finish. Pause only if catastrophic. Write 3 weak spots after.

lessons.title: Record your mix
lessons.summary: Record a continuous mix in your DJ software (or system audio). Keep going through mistakes.

exercise.title: Record take 1
exercise.description: Record 10–15 minutes. Save the file with date in the name.

lessons.title: Critical listen and fix list
lessons.summary: Listen next day if possible. Mark timestamps for trainwrecks, double bass, abrupt cuts.

exercise.title: Three improvements
exercise.description: Write exactly 3 timestamped improvements for take 2.

checklist: One thing that already worked noted

lessons.title: Second take
lessons.summary: Re-record implementing the fix list. Do not chase perfection beyond take 2 for this milestone.

exercise.title: Record take 2
exercise.description: Apply fixes; record again; keep the better take.

lessons.title: Share safely
lessons.summary: Optional: share with a trusted friend for feedback. Private link fine. No need for public release.

exercise.title: Optional share + reflection
exercise.description: Share or skip. Write 5 sentences: what you learned about beatmatching, phrasing, EQ, nerves, next goal.

checklist: Next DJ goal chosen (e.g. longer set / new genre)

modules.title: Production Capstone: First Finished Track
modules.description: Arrange, mix lightly, reference, export, and decide what's next.

lessons.title: Arrangement template
lessons.summary: Expand your 32-bar sketch into a full mini-track: intro, verse/groove, build, drop/main, outro (adapt names to your genre).

exercise.title: Fill the template
exercise.description: Aim 2–3 minutes. Copy sections; change one element per section.

lessons.title: Fill gaps (FX, risers, silence)
lessons.summary: Transitions between sections need glue: reverse cymbals, noise risers, drums dropping out, or intentional silence.

exercise.title: Three transitions
exercise.description: Add or simplify 3 section transitions. Remove anything that clutters.

checklist: At least one moment of reduced elements

lessons.title: Mix: levels and EQ carve
lessons.summary: Static mix: faders first, then small EQ cuts for clash (especially kick vs bass, vocal vs synth if any).
whyItMatters: Clear kick+bass is the beginner win condition.

exercise.title: Static mix pass
exercise.description: Mix in mono briefly if available; ensure kick and bass readable; tame harsh highs.

checklist: EQ cuts used more than boosts

lessons.title: Space: reverb and delay sparingly
lessons.summary: One shared reverb send often beats unique reverbs on every track. Keep dry punch on kick.

exercise.title: One send reverb
exercise.description: Put short/medium reverb on hats or melody via send; keep kick dry.

lessons.title: Reference track A/B
lessons.summary: A/B against one commercial track in a similar genre/loudness neighborhood (turn yours up/down to compare tone, not ego loudness).
whyItMatters: Shows missing bass or harshness fast.

exercise.title: A/B notes
exercise.description: Import or play a reference. Write 3 gaps (e.g. my hats louder, my bass thinner).

lessons.title: Export and listen on 2 devices
lessons.summary: Export WAV + MP3. Listen on phone and headphones/laptop. Note fixes for a future revision — but declare v1 finished.

exercise.title: Ship v1
exercise.description: Export, listen on 2 devices, keep a short fix list for later, celebrate.

lessons.title: What's next
lessons.summary: Options: DJ your own track, try a new genre, revisit ear training, explore Learning Synths, or follow a longer free course (e.g. freeCodeCamp) now that fundamentals stick.
whyItMatters: Loops you back into BeatPath drills.

exercise.title: Pick next focus
exercise.description: Choose one: genre deep-dive, DJ Track if unfinished, weekly ear drills, or a guided video course.

lessons.successCheckpoint: Production path complete for v1 goals

glossarySeed.definition: Beats per minute — the speed of the pulse.
A group of beats; in 4/4, usually 4 beats.
A musical sentence, often 8 or 16 bars in dance music.
A saved position in a track you can jump to quickly.
Control that speeds up or slows down a deck to match tempo.
Aligning tempo and beats of two tracks so they play in sync.
Equalizer — turns bass/mids/highs up or down.
Slider that blends audible output from one deck toward the other.
A curated set of tracks for a session or vibe.
Digital Audio Workstation — software for recording and producing music.
Data for notes and performance; drives virtual instruments.
Recorded or imported sound on the timeline.
Using one sound (often kick) to automatically lower another (often bass).
Distortion from signal going above maximum level.
WAV is uncompressed audio; MP3 is compressed for smaller files.
The tonal center / scale a piece lives in.
DJ software feature that auto-matches tempo (and sometimes beats).
Quick-jump marker for drops, vocals, or loops.
A repeating section; often 4 or 8 bars.
Opening and closing sections often used for mixing.
High-energy section after a build/break.
Input level control before the channel fader.
Previewing a track in headphones without sending it to the master.
The main output the audience hears.
Timing shift that delays certain subdivisions for groove.
Quiet extra hit that adds feel.
Five-note scale; friendly for beginners.
Shared path for effects like reverb used by multiple tracks.
A commercial song used to compare your mix tone and balance.
Slang for a badly aligned mix where beats collide messily.
Kick drum on every beat (1-2-3-4).
Snare/clap emphasis on beats 2 and 4.
How low or high a sound is; measured in Hz.
Unclear low-mids from too many competing sounds.
Hardware with knobs/pads/faders that controls DJ or DAW software.
Hardware that gets sound in/out of a computer with better quality than basic laptop jacks.
Effects and instruments included free with your DAW.
Licenses that allow use of samples without paying royalties (always read terms).
How sections are ordered and varied over time.
Deliberate practice — short, focused, repeated (word borrowed from Indian classical tradition).

gearTiers.title: ₹0 — Skills first
items: Laptop or desktop you already have
One free DAW (LMMS / Cakewalk / Waveform Free)
gearTiers.note: Do not buy a controller until you finished Module M5 drills.

gearTiers.title: ~₹2,000–5,000 — Hear better
items: Notebook for set cards and arrangement notes
gearTiers.note: Hearing detail matters more than RGB pads.

gearTiers.title: ~₹5,000–15,000 — Hands-on or cleaner audio
items: Used/entry DJ controller (Numark-class) OR entry audio interface
Monitor speakers only if room is quiet — headphones still OK
gearTiers.note: Pick controller if DJ path is primary; interface if recording vocals/instruments.

gearTiers.title: ~₹25,000–40,000 — When skills are solid
items: Pioneer DDJ-FLX4-class dual-deck controller (check current India street prices)
Better headphones or entry monitors + basic treatment (blankets/books first)
gearTiers.note: Buy after you recorded at least one mix and/or one track you are proud of.

dj.name: Mixxx
dj.notes: Best zero-rupee learning default; full features.

dj.name: rekordbox
dj.notes: Strong with Pioneer gear; good library tools.

dj.name: VirtualDJ Home
dj.notes: Accessible UI; check license for public use.

daw.name: Cakewalk
daw.notes: Full studio features for Windows users.

daw.name: Audacity
daw.notes: Editing/recording helper, not a full beat DAW.

daw.name: Reaper
daw.notes: Powerful and lightweight; pay when evaluating ends.

daw.name: FL Studio
daw.notes: Very popular for beats; freeCodeCamp course uses it.

daw.name: Ableton Live
daw.notes: Session view great for ideas; Learning Music pairs well.

daw.name: openDAW
daw.notes: Educational web DAW to explore; not a full offline replacement yet.

todayPracticeAlgorithm.description: Pick next incomplete lesson in focus track; after Shared exam (m3.l5), allow DJ or Production focus. Append one rotating drill from completed modules targeting 15–30 minutes total.
